subject: Payload windowing & tail latency — tradeoffs and next steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.inference.com>

Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.inference.com>, Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.inference.com>
Date: Tue, 01 Sep 2026 15:04:00 -0700
Subject: Payload windowing & tail latency — tradeoffs and next steps

Hi Alicia — thanks again for the demo and the deep dive today. Quick recap from my side and a proposed plan so we can scope a short PoC next week.

Summary of what we heard on the call:
- Primary UX: progressive answer streaming for user-facing search/assist flows. Partial outputs must arrive as tokens are generated.
- Latency targets: p50 ~ <80ms for short prompts (<=200 tokens); p99 target for short prompts: ~250ms. For long-form generation (input > 800 tokens or outputs > 400 tokens) you are OK with higher p99 (~700–900ms) if streaming is steady.
- Typical payload mix: ~60% short (<200 tokens), 25% medium (200–800 tokens), 15% long (>800 tokens).
- Concurrency: sustained target ~50 concurrent sessions during peak with occasional spikes to 120.
- Failure mode tolerance: you prefer graceful degradation (partial streaming + async completion) over outright throttling.

Open/clarifying items we need from you (please reply inline):
1) Do you have an SLA requirement around p95/p99 cost of failure (e.g., credits or escalation)?
2) For streaming, do your clients use a hard SSE path (keep-alive) or do you prefer chunked HTTP responses?
3) Can you share 10–20 representative payloads (redacted) so we can run tokenization and KV-cache sizing?

Proposed next steps from Redwood:
- Rishi to propose a short PoC configuration: dedicated small pool (reserved capacity) + quantized model variant, and a routing policy that prioritizes short prompt latency.
- Dev to produce an initial estimate for KV cache sizing and memory requirements for your long inputs.
- Marissa to coordinate a 90-minute PoC kick-off and sign the PoC statement of work.

Attachments: call-notes-20260901.pdf (notes + transcript), sample-prompt-set.jsonl (example payloads)

Thanks — I’ll schedule the kickoff once you confirm availability.

Best,
Marissa

Hi Marissa — thanks for the clear recap. A few clarifications inline:

> 1) SLA requirement?
We don't have a formal customer-facing SLA yet; for now our procurement team will want a clear escalation path and credits tied to p99 breaches for the top-tier customers. I'll loop Procurement if we get to contract.

> 2) Streaming protocol?
We currently use chunked HTTP for web clients and SSE for our mobile clients. We need consistent behavior across both (i.e., partial tokens should not arrive out of order).

> 3) Payloads?
Attached: payload-examples.zip — contains 25 anonymized request examples. Note: some 'long' payloads include embedded context from a knowledge base (~1,500 tokens) and we cannot truncate those on the client.

Tolerance for latency: for short flows we want p99 <= 300ms end-to-end. For long flows, we accept up to ~1.0s p99 if streaming delivers steady token chunks and first token appears quickly (first-byte latency). We are fine with higher p50 values for long jobs.

We can do the PoC next week — Thurs/Friday mornings preferred PT. Please share the PoC success criteria and proposed test harness.

Thanks,
Alicia

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.inference.com>

Cc: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.inference.com>
Date: Fri, 04 Sep 2026 11:38:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Payload windowing & tail latency — tradeoffs and next steps

Alicia / Marissa — quick technical response and three pragmatic options we should evaluate in the PoC. I also attached a short spreadsheet (poc_sla_options.xlsx) with rough perf estimates.

Background assumptions (from our end):
- Model family: mid-sized open decoder (optimized variant available).
- We can provision a dedicated pool that prioritizes low-latency routing for short prompts and sends long prompts through a separate worker pool that supports streaming + KV caching.

Options to evaluate (pros/cons):
1) Low-latency fast path (preferred for short prompts)
   - Dedicated small-batch runtime with immediate dispatch (no batching > 4 requests), 4-bit quantized model variant, reserved concurrency 60.
   - Expected: first-token latency ~60–120ms; p99 for short prompts ~180–300ms depending on network.
   - Tradeoff: less throughput efficiency, higher cost per token.

2) Mixed routing with streaming for long jobs
   - Long inputs (>800 tokens) routed to streaming-optimized lane: aggressive KV caching, chunked generation to client, can accept higher p99 (700–1000ms) but steady streaming.
   - We can implement partial-response checkpoints so the client gets usable content early and we continue background generation for completion.

3) Cost-first fallback (if under load)
   - If cluster saturates, fallback to a smaller quantized model that returns a shortened/abridged response (or an async continuation link).
   - Tradeoff: potential quality degradation; simpler to implement than complex sharding or autoscaling.

Metrics & PoC plan (what we'll measure):
- p50/p95/p99 for first-token and full-response for three payload classes (short/medium/long).
- Throughput: sustained 50 concurrent sessions for 30 minutes and spike test to 120 concurrent sessions for 5 minutes.
- Streaming health: median inter-chunk latency and first-byte latency.
- Error/failure rate: timeouts, truncations, and fallback invocations.

Acceptance criteria (proposal):
- Short prompts: p99 first-token <= 300ms, error rate < 0.5%.
- Medium/long prompts: first-token <= 500ms for medium, <= 800ms for long; streaming must deliver subsequent chunks at steady pace (90th percentile inter-chunk < 200ms).

Next steps I need from Giganto:
- Confirm sample payloads are representative (thank you for the zip).
- Approve PoC window and allow synthetic load tests.

I can lead the PoC technical kickoff. If agreed, I'll prepare a simple harness (k6 + tokenized payloads) and a short runbook.

-Rishi
